critic_changes: Checked every cited URL. All pages exist on tier 1 domains (adb.org, imf.org, worldbank.org subdomains), and all quoted passages appear on them. The PDFs were read from their extracted text.

Banking thread: removed the claim that the Bendigo Bank agency opened in 2015, because no cited page says so. Removed 'said in 2023', because the quote does not carry it. Added an IMF 2023 passage that supports 'Nauru's only bank'.

Trust funds thread: removed 'could then neither service foreign loans nor fully pay for services' and 'elected in 2004', because no cited passage covers them. Reworded 'stopped working and closed for good in 2006' to 'closed in 2006' to match the ADB passage. The ADB 2007 report dates the bank's halt to 1998, and the IMF dates its liquidation to 2016.

Processing centre thread: the ADB passage cited only showed that a contraction was avoided, not that centre revenue was the main source of public money. Lengthened it (to 25 words) to include RPC revenue enabling the spending and its share of revenues and grants. The text now says this held by FY2022–FY2023.

World Bank MPO citation: corrected the title. The URL is the full October 2024 Macro Poverty Outlook (Annual Meetings 2024), not a standalone Central Pacific Islands note. Date 2024-10 confirmed, and the quote was found in the Central Pacific Islands section.

Revenue base thread: dropped 'donor grants' from the list of revenue sources, because the IMF passage names fishing licence fees, residual phosphate processing and the RPC. Lengthened the World Bank 2026 passage so it supports the cause of the surplus fall (rising social costs as well as falling fishing licence and grant revenue), and the text now says so.

Headline: 'two decades of decline' became 'decades of decline', because income per person fell every year from 1976 to 2002. 'Revived income per person after 2012' became a mining restart plus the processing centre, because the 8.4 percent era starts in 2008 and the ADB dates the mining restart to FY2007.
Tension: softened 'growth in FY2022 driven by strong phosphate production' to 'helped growth', because the IMF says phosphate production and fiscal support partly offset a weak transport sector.

growth_story.headline: Phosphate wealth collapsed into decades of decline; a mining restart and a refugee processing centre lifted income per person, but growth has slowed since 2016.
growth_story.arc: Income per person peaked in 1975 on phosphate exports and is now 80.9 percent below that peak, lower even than in 1970. From 1990 to 1998 it fell 11.8 percent a year as phosphate mining declined and the government borrowed against its trust funds to pay running costs until the assets ran out. The fall slowed to 5.1 percent a year in 1999–2007, years of a failed national bank, a sovereign default in 2004 and an Australian-funded refugee processing centre under a 2002 agreement. Growth turned to 8.4 percent a year in 2008–2015, after phosphate mining restarted on a small scale in FY2007 and Australia set up a regional processing centre in 2012, with jumps of 22.3 percent in 2012 and 13.4 in 2014. Since 2016 growth has averaged 0.8 percent a year, against 5.4 in the decade before, as income came to rest on the processing centre, fishing licence fees and donor grants.

threads.title: Phosphate wealth runs out
threads.text: Phosphate exports built large offshore assets, but mining began to decline in the late 1980s and the deposits were largely used up by the late 1990s. Income per person fell every year from 1976 to 2002.

threads.title: The processing centre economy
threads.text: Australia set up a regional processing centre for asylum seekers in September 2012. By FY2022–FY2023 its revenue made up most of government revenue and grants, and it paid for the higher spending that kept the economy from shrinking during the pandemic. The centre was due to go on standby in 2023 but was renewed in 2024.

threads.title: A narrow, volatile revenue base
threads.text: Apart from the centre, public revenue rests on fishing licence fees and what is left of phosphate processing. Mining has degraded much of the island and pushed people onto a narrow coastal strip. In the latest year, rising social spending and falling fishing licence and grant revenue cut the budget surplus sharply.

In May 2026 the World Bank described growth as modest but positive, helped by port and solar projects, and projected a sharp slowdown as processing-centre revenue declines. Income per person grew 1.5 percent in 2025.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe processing-centre revenue rising steeply into FY2022–FY2023, and the IMF says strong phosphate production helped growth in FY2022. Yet income per person fell in 2022 and 2023 (-0.8 and -1.3 percent) and grew only 0.8 percent a year over 2016–2025. The sources mostly track government revenue and total output by fiscal year, while the data track income per person by calendar year, so a revenue boom shows up only weakly in the series.
